title: The Boy With No Shadow
summary: Pip trades his own shadow for a whole day of luck — and at first it's wonderful. But a shadow does more than we imagine, and without his, Pip begins to grow too light, too forgotten, almost transparent. To get it back, he has to understand why the shadow followed him.

chapters.title: The Noon Trade
chapters.body:
Pip was ten years old and had a theory: luck was handed out unfairly, and he had ended up in the wrong line.

Not that his life was bad. But Pip was one of those boys for whom everything goes a little bit wrong. The toast fell butter-side down. The line he chose was always the slowest. When they drew pairs at school, he was the one left over. Nothing tragic — just an endless string of small misfortunes that, added up, made Pip believe he'd been born with no luck at all.

It was at noon on a hot day, when shadows shrink to little pools beneath your feet, that the man appeared in the square. He was thin and tall, dressed in grey, with a smile that looked painted on. And he had a little stall with a sign that read: LUCK TRADED. ASK HOW.

Pip asked how.

"Simple," said the grey man, and his voice was smooth as soap. "You give me something you don't use for anything, and I give you a whole day of luck. Real luck. Everything goes right, from sunrise to sunset."

"Something I don't use?" Pip frowned. "Like what?"

The man pointed at the ground, at Pip's feet, where the short noon shadow huddled.

"Your shadow," he said. "Tell me: what does it do for you? Nothing. It follows you all day, gets in the way, falls over things, darkens what you want to see. A shadow is dead weight. You wouldn't even miss it." The painted smile stretched. "Give me your shadow, and I'll give you a day of perfect luck. Fair, isn't it? You trade what's useless for what you always wanted."

And Pip — who was ten years old and had a theory about the unfairness of luck — thought it was the best deal in the world. What did a shadow do, after all? Nothing at all. It only followed him.

"Done," said Pip.

The grey man bent down, and with a quick gesture, like someone peeling off a sticker, he unstuck Pip's shadow from the ground. It was a strange sensation — a little tug at the soles of his feet, and then an odd lightness, like taking off a heavy backpack. The man rolled up Pip's shadow like a cloth, tucked it into his pocket, and handed Pip a small, warm coin.

"Good for one day of luck," he said. "It starts now. Enjoy it." And, folding up his stall, he added, almost too low for Pip to hear: "They always enjoy it. It's the part I like best. The before."

Pip didn't even notice the phrase. He was already running across the square, feeling light and lucky, hardly able to wait to see what perfect luck would bring.

chapters.title: Too Light
chapters.body:
The day of luck was everything the man had promised.

Pip found a coin on the sidewalk. Then another. The ice-cream man gave him an extra scoop "just because." He got every question right at school without studying. The boy who always picked on him slipped in a puddle and Pip walked past untouched. Everything, absolutely everything, went right. For the first time in his life, Pip was in the right line.

But as the afternoon wore on, he began to notice strange things.

The first was at the candy shop. Pip picked out a lollipop, went to pay, and the shopkeeper looked at him with a puzzled face.

"Were you here, boy?" the man asked. "Sorry, I didn't see you come in."

Pip laughed, thought it was absent-mindedness. But it happened again. And again. People stopped noticing him. He'd speak and they'd be slow to answer, as if his voice arrived muffled. A woman nearly bumped into him on the street and startled, as if Pip had appeared out of nowhere. It was as if, without his shadow, Pip were becoming hard to see.

The second strange thing was the forgetting. Not his — other people's. A classmate had greeted him that morning, cheerful, and by afternoon looked at Pip without quite recognizing him, frowning like someone trying to recall a name. His own mother, when Pip got home, took a moment longer to smile, a moment in which her eyes passed over him as if searching for someone.

And the third thing — the most frightening — Pip felt on the inside. He was growing light. Too light. Not only his body: his thoughts, his memories. It was as if, without the shadow stuck to him, something that held him firm in the world were coming loose. He looked at his own hands at dusk and — he could have sworn — you could see a little of the wall through them.

Pip began to understand, with a chill in his belly, what he had done. The grey man had said the shadow was good for nothing. But that was a lie. The shadow was good for one thing no one notices precisely because it never fails: the shadow is the proof that we are real. It's what tells the world, the sun, other people, the ground: I am here, I have weight, I am real. Without a shadow, Pip was becoming a rumor of himself. A person the light passed through. A boy the world was, slowly, forgetting to keep.

And the lighter he grew, the more he missed the small misfortunes he had so hated — because Pip realized, too late, that tripping, being left over, choosing the wrong line, all of that was proof that he existed, that he bumped into the world, that the world bumped into him. Perfect luck was no fun at all when no one could see you winning.

The sun was setting. And Pip knew, with an icy certainty, that when the last light of day faded — when there was no more sun even to try to cast the shadow he didn't have — he would fade too. Too light. Too forgotten. Erased.

He ran for the square, hoping the grey man was still there.

chapters.title: What the Shadow Carried
chapters.body:
The grey man was still in the square, folding the last cloths of his stall, in no hurry, like someone waiting.

"Ah," he said, seeing Pip come running, already half transparent in the orange light of late afternoon. "The boy who asks the questions after. They always come back at this hour. Right when the sun goes away." The painted smile stretched. "You want your shadow back, I imagine."

"I do," Pip panted. "Here's the coin. Give me back my shadow."

The grey man shook his head, slowly.

"It doesn't work that way. The luck's already been used, the whole day. The coin's worth nothing now." He shrugged. "But I'm fair. I can give your shadow back, yes. Only now it costs more than an old coin. It costs another shadow." His eyes gleamed. "Bring me someone else's shadow. Anyone's. A friend, your mother. Tell me their name and point, and I'll take their shadow and give you back yours. They'll go light like you are, forgotten, fading — but you become real again. You just pass it along. Most pass it along. It's astonishing how, when they're fading, most pass it along."

And here was the real trap, the one the coin had only opened: it wasn't enough that Pip had been foolish. Now they were offering him the chance to condemn someone else to what he was feeling, and calling it a repair.

Pip thought of his mother. He thought of how easy it would be to say her name, to point, and go back to being seen, to being remembered, to having weight. And he thought of her afterward — too light, passed through by the light, forgotten by all, fading at sunset the way he was about to fade.

"No," said Pip.

The grey man raised a painted eyebrow.

"No? You'd rather fade? When the sun sets, minutes from now, you're finished. No one will remember you existed. That's the price of your 'no.'"

"I'd rather fade than make my mother fade," said Pip, and his voice trembled, and he was truly afraid, but he did not take it back. "You said most pass it along. I'm not going to be most. If I have to go, I'll go. But I'm not taking anyone with me."

And then something happened that made the grey man's painted smile falter for the first time.

On the ground, at his feet, the pocket where he kept the stolen shadows began to stir. And Pip's shadow — folded in there for hours — slipped out. Not because the man let it go. Because a shadow, at bottom, is the proof that we are real — and Pip, by refusing to steal someone else's reality to save his own, had just proven that he was real in a way no trade could undo. He had weight. Real weight. The weight of someone who chooses the hard right over the easy wrong. And a shadow always comes back to whoever has that weight.

Pip's shadow slid across the ground of the square, quick, and stuck itself back to his feet, in the exact place it had come from. And at once Pip felt it all return — the good weight in his body, the firmness in his thoughts, the certainty of being real. His hands became solid again. He was whole again.

The grey man recoiled, and the painted smile was gone.

"Keep your shadow, then," he said, and the smooth voice was sour. "And keep your bad luck with it. You'll have plenty."

"Good," said Pip, and to his own surprise, he meant it. "Every stumble is proof that I'm here. I found out today that I'd rather have a life full of toast falling on the floor than a day of luck where no one sees me." He dropped the dead coin on the ground of the square. "Keep it. I've already got what I needed."

And Pip went home, stepping firmly, happy with his own weight, happy even with the long shadow the setting sun stretched behind him across the ground — the shadow that followed him not to get in the way, he understood now, but to remind the whole world, with every step, that here went a real boy.

His mother opened the door before he even knocked, and her hug was firm and long and full of recognition, without that moment of searching for someone. And that night, when Pip knocked over his glass of milk at the table — because he was still Pip, and his luck was still crooked — he laughed. He laughed for real. Because a spilled glass, he had learned, is a thing that only happens to people who exist.
